_about: Device atlas: one entry per transistor type, used by site/devices.html (animations + band diagrams), sim/transistor_sim/bandatlas.py and docs/20-how-transistors-work.md. Band-model parameters are schematic but physically ordered; see bandatlas.py.

devices.name: Point-contact transistor
devices.summary: Two gold contacts 50 µm apart press on n-type germanium. Forward-biasing the emitter injects holes into a thin surface layer; the reverse-biased collector sweeps them up, and a small emitter current controls a larger collector voltage swing.

steps.text: Emitter unbiased: the barrier between emitter and germanium blocks hole injection; only a tiny leakage reaches the collector.
Forward-bias the emitter a little: holes start to spill over the lowered barrier into the n-type surface layer.
Holes drift and diffuse ~50 µm to the collector point, whose reverse bias pulls them in: collector current follows emitter current.
Because the collector sits at a much higher voltage, the same current delivers more power there than the emitter consumed: gain.

devices.where: Museums: replaced within a decade by junction transistors, which were far more reproducible.

devices.name: Bipolar junction transistor (npn)
devices.summary: A thin p-type base sits between an n⁺ emitter and an n collector. The base–emitter voltage lowers the barrier for electrons exponentially; almost all injected electrons cross the thin base and fall into the collector.

steps.text: V_BE = 0: the emitter–base junction is at equilibrium and its built-in barrier (~0.9 eV) keeps electrons in the emitter.
Raise V_BE: the barrier drops by qV_BE and electron injection grows tenfold every 60 mV — the Boltzmann factor.
Injected electrons diffuse across the thin base faster than they recombine, then drop down the collector junction's field.
Base current (holes back-injected into the emitter) is ~100× smaller than collector current: current gain β ≈ 100.

devices.where: Analog and RF circuits, bandgap references, power amplifiers; the core of 1960s–80s logic (TTL, ECL).

devices.name: Heterojunction bipolar transistor (SiGe / InP)
devices.who: Concept: H. Kroemer (1957); SiGe HBTs: IBM (late 1980s)
devices.summary: A narrower-gap base (SiGe, or InGaAs in InP HBTs) creates a valence-band step that blocks holes from flowing back into the emitter. The base can then be heavily doped and very thin, reaching hundreds of GHz.

steps.text: Off: the emitter–base barrier holds electrons back, exactly as in a BJT.
Forward bias injects electrons into the base; the extra valence-band step ΔE_v blocks holes from going the other way.
Because back-injection is suppressed by e^{ΔE_v/kT}, the base can be doped 100× harder and made only ~10–20 nm thick.
A thin, low-resistance base means transit times of picoseconds: f_T and f_max of 300–700 GHz in modern SiGe and InP HBTs.

devices.where: 5G and satellite radios, automotive radar, 100G+ optical-fibre drivers.

devices.name: Junction field-effect transistor
devices.who: W. Shockley (theory 1952); G. Dacey, I. Ross (1953)
devices.summary: Current flows through an n-type channel between two p⁺ gate junctions. Reverse-biasing the gate widens the depletion regions until they meet and pinch the channel off. It is normally on.

steps.text: V_GS = 0: the channel is wide open and electrons flow freely from source to drain.
Make the gate negative: the reverse-biased junctions grow their depletion regions into the channel, narrowing it.
At the pinch-off voltage the depletion regions meet and the channel closes.
With drain voltage the channel pinches near the drain first, so the current saturates, like a MOSFET.

devices.where: Low-noise audio and instrument front ends, ultra-high-impedance inputs; SiC JFETs in power switching.

devices.name: GaAs MESFET
devices.who: C. Mead (Caltech, 1966); first GaAs MESFET: W. Hooper, W. Lehrer (1967)
devices.summary: GaAs has no good native oxide, so the gate is a metal Schottky contact directly on a thin n-type channel. The Schottky depletion region replaces the JFET's p-n junction; GaAs's light electrons make it fast.

steps.text: V_GS ≈ 0: a thin depletion region under the Schottky gate leaves most of the n-GaAs channel open.
Negative gate voltage deepens the depletion region into the channel.
When depletion reaches the semi-insulating substrate the channel is cut off.
Electrons (m* = 0.067 m₀) cross sub-micron gates in picoseconds: the first microwave transistors for satellites and radar.

devices.where: Early cell-phone and satellite amplifiers; mostly replaced by HEMTs and HBTs.

devices.name: Planar MOSFET (bulk silicon)
devices.summary: A gate on thin oxide pulls electrons to the surface of p-type silicon, forming an inversion layer that connects source and drain. From 1970 to 2011 this flat design, shrunk from 10 µm to 32 nm, built the digital world.

steps.text: Gate below V_T: a potential barrier between source and channel keeps the source's electrons out.
Near threshold the barrier drops as the gate bends the bands; current rises one decade per ~85 mV (n ≈ 1.4).
Above V_T the surface inverts: an electron sheet connects source to drain and current flows by drift.
At high drain voltage the channel pinches off near the drain and the drain also lowers the source barrier (DIBL), the weakness that ended planar scaling.

devices.where: Everything digital from the 4004 to 32 nm CPUs; still in analog, sensors and power management.

devices.name: Fully depleted SOI MOSFET
devices.who: Research: J.-P. Colinge and others; production: STMicroelectronics, GlobalFoundries (28/22 nm)
devices.summary: The channel is an ultra-thin silicon film (~7 nm) on a buried oxide. There is no deep silicon below for the drain's field to leak through, and the substrate can act as a second 'back gate' to tune the threshold.

steps.text: Off: the whole thin film is depleted and its barrier is held up by the gate from above and the buried oxide below.
Because no deep depletion region soaks up gate charge, the swing is steeper (~65–70 mV/dec).
Above threshold electrons fill the film; the undoped channel avoids random-dopant variation.
A back-gate bias on the substrate shifts V_T by ~80 mV/V, trading speed against leakage on the fly.

devices.where: Low-power IoT, automotive radar, RF SoCs (GlobalFoundries 22FDX, ST 28/18 nm).

devices.name: FinFET (tri-gate)
devices.who: D. Hisamoto, C. Hu et al. (1998–2000); first in production: Intel 22 nm (2011)
devices.summary: The channel stands up as a thin fin and the gate wraps its top and both sides. Gating from three sides shrinks the electrostatic natural length, so the gate keeps control at ~20 nm lengths where planar devices leaked.

steps.text: Off: gates on both sides hold the whole fin's barrier high; the drain barely reaches the source.
The fin is fully depleted and gated from both sides, so the swing is close to the 60 mV/dec limit (~65–70 mV/dec).
Above threshold electrons fill the fin volume; several fins in parallel make one wider transistor.
DIBL stays near 30–50 mV/V, about three times better than planar at the same gate length.

devices.where: Every leading CPU, GPU and phone chip from 2011 to 2024.

devices.name: Gate-all-around nanosheet
devices.who: Research: IBM, imec (2017); production: Samsung 3 nm (2022), TSMC N2 and Intel 18A (2025)
devices.summary: Three or four horizontal silicon sheets, each ~5 nm thick, are stacked and completely surrounded by the gate. Four-sided control is the best electrostatics silicon can get, and the sheet width can be tuned per transistor.

steps.text: Off: the gate surrounds each sheet, so its barrier is controlled from every side; leakage paths through the body are gone.
Swing ≈ 62–65 mV/dec, within a few percent of the thermal limit.
Electrons flow through all stacked sheets in parallel; wider sheets give more current per footprint than fins.
DIBL ~20–30 mV/V, so gates of ~12–15 nm hold off the drain. Quantum confinement in 5 nm sheets shifts V_T (Lab 08).

devices.where: 2 nm-class chips from late 2025; the base for CFET and IBM's 0.7 nm nanostack.

devices.name: Complementary FET (stacked nFET/pFET)
devices.who: imec (roadmap, 2018); research demos by IBM, Intel, TSMC
devices.summary: The pFET nanosheets are stacked directly on top of the nFET nanosheets under one gate, so a CMOS inverter uses the footprint of one transistor. The band diagram shows the nFET tier; the pFET above mirrors it with holes.

steps.text: Input low: the bottom nFET's barrier is high (off) while the top pFET is on, pulling the output high.
As the shared gate rises the nFET barrier falls and the pFET barrier rises: the inverter switches.
Input high: nFET on, pFET off — the output is pulled to ground through the bottom tier.
Stacking halves the cell area of a logic gate; the price is harder processing and heat trapped in the stack.

devices.where: Future logic nodes beyond ~1 nm-class naming.

devices.name: AlGaN/GaN HEMT
devices.who: Concept: T. Mimura (GaAs, 1980); first AlGaN/GaN HEMT: M. A. Khan et al. (1993)
devices.summary: Polarization charge at the AlGaN/GaN interface creates a sheet of ~10¹³ electrons/cm² with no doping — a two-dimensional electron gas with high mobility. A negative gate voltage lifts the triangular well above the Fermi level to switch it off.

steps.text: V_GS = 0: the polarization-induced well dips below E_F and fills with a 2DEG; the transistor is normally on.
A negative gate lifts the AlGaN and the well; subbands rise toward E_F and the sheet density falls.
Past the pinch-off voltage (~−3 to −4 V) the ground subband is above E_F: channel empty.
The wide 3.4 eV gap lets the drain hold hundreds of volts; high density × mobility gives high current. Heat is the limit (Lab 11).

devices.where: 5G base stations, radar, phone and laptop fast chargers, data-centre power supplies.

devices.name: SiC power MOSFET (vertical)
devices.who: Cree/Wolfspeed first commercial (2011); B. J. Baliga's figure of merit (1982)
devices.summary: Current flows through a short MOS channel at the surface of the p-body, then vertically down a thick, lightly doped n⁻ drift layer to the drain on the back. SiC's 10× higher breakdown field lets the drift layer be 10× thinner than silicon's for the same voltage.

steps.text: Off: the p-body blocks electrons; the drain voltage is held by the depleted n⁻ drift layer below.
Gate voltage inverts the p-body surface; SiC's rough SiC/SiO₂ interface makes this channel less mobile than silicon's.
Electrons cross the channel, turn downward and cross ~10 µm of drift layer to the backside drain.
The blocking layer is thin and doped 100× more than a silicon device of the same rating, so on-resistance is far lower at 650–3300 V.

devices.where: Electric-vehicle traction inverters and chargers, solar inverters, rail.

devices.name: Insulated-gate bipolar transistor
devices.summary: A MOSFET on top, a bipolar p⁺ layer at the bottom. When the MOS channel turns on, electrons flow down and trigger hole injection from the p⁺ collector; the drift region floods with both carriers (conductivity modulation), so it conducts far better than a MOSFET's.

steps.text: Gate off: no MOS channel, so no electron flow; the thick drift region holds the voltage.
Gate above V_T: electrons enter the drift region through the channel.
Those electrons forward-bias the bottom p⁺/n junction, which injects holes: the drift region fills with electron–hole plasma.
Low on-voltage at high current; the stored holes must be removed at turn-off, which limits switching speed (the 'tail current').

devices.where: Trains, industrial drives, wind turbines, many EV inverters, induction cooktops.

devices.name: Hydrogen-terminated diamond FET
devices.who: H. Kawarada et al. (Waseda, 1994); transfer doping: F. Maier et al. (2000)
devices.summary: Diamond is nearly impossible to dope usefully, but a hydrogen-terminated surface under air or Al₂O₃ loses electrons to acceptors outside the crystal. A 2D hole gas ~1 nm deep forms: a p-channel with no dopants in the diamond at all.

steps.text: V_GS = 0: surface transfer doping has bent the valence band above E_F at the surface — a 2D hole gas conducts.
Positive gate voltage pushes the valence band back down and depletes the holes.
When the surface valence band sits below E_F the hole gas is gone: off (hole devices switch the opposite way).
Diamond's 10 MV/cm breakdown field and 2000 W/m·K conductivity promise extreme voltage and heat tolerance.

devices.where: Research and early commercial power/RF parts (Japanese start-ups, 2025).

devices.name: Monolayer MoS₂ FET
devices.who: B. Radisavljevic, A. Kis et al. (EPFL, 2011); 0.42 nm AlOx interface: NYCU + TSMC (2026)
devices.summary: The channel is a single molecular layer of MoS₂, 0.65 nm thick, with no dangling bonds. The gate controls every atom of the channel, so short-channel effects are tiny; the challenges are contacts, interfaces and wafer-scale growth.

steps.text: Off: the 1.8 eV gap and atomically thin body keep leakage very low.
The body is thinner than any silicon sheet, so the natural length λ is tiny and the swing stays near 60–70 mV/dec.
Electrons accumulate in the sheet; mobility (~50–200 cm²/V·s) is lower than silicon's but degrades less with thinness.
Engineering the gate interface (the 0.42 nm AlOx layer) and metal contacts decides whether 2D channels beat silicon.

devices.where: Research; candidate channel beyond silicon nanosheets (IRDS roadmap, 2030s).

devices.name: Carbon-nanotube FET
devices.who: S. Tans, A. Verschueren, C. Dekker (Delft, 1998); RV16X-NANO CPU: MIT (2019)
devices.summary: A single semiconducting nanotube ~1.5 nm across bridges two metal contacts. Where metal meets tube a Schottky barrier forms; the gate thins that barrier until electrons tunnel through, so a CNT FET switches at the contacts, not in the middle.

steps.text: Off: the tube's bands sit high; electrons from the metal face a tall, thick Schottky barrier.
The gate pushes the tube's bands down; the barrier at each contact becomes a thin spike.
Electrons tunnel through the thin spike and cross the nearly ballistic tube (mean free path ~100s of nm).
Promise: ballistic transport and ~3× energy efficiency; problems: purity (metallic tubes), placement and contacts.

devices.where: Research; monolithic 3D chips and flexible electronics.

devices.name: Tunnel FET
devices.who: Band-to-band tunnelling: L. Esaki (1958); TFET review: A. Ionescu, H. Riel (2011)
devices.summary: Instead of lifting electrons over a barrier (which can't switch faster than 60 mV/decade), the gate pulls the channel's conduction band below the source's valence band so electrons tunnel straight through the gap. The turn-on can be steeper than the thermal limit.

steps.text: Off: the channel conduction band sits above the source valence band — no empty states at the same energy, so no tunnelling.
Raising the gate lowers the channel bands; an energy window opens between source E_v and channel E_c.
Electrons tunnel horizontally from the source valence band into the channel conduction band and flow to the drain.
Because the window opens abruptly, swing can beat 60 mV/dec — but tunnelling currents are small (Chapter 15).

devices.name: IGZO thin-film transistor
devices.who: K. Nomura, H. Hosono et al. (Tokyo Tech, 2004)
devices.summary: An amorphous indium–gallium–zinc oxide film deposited at low temperature on glass or plastic, gated from below. Its wide gap gives extremely low leakage, and its mobility (~10 cm²/V·s) beats amorphous silicon's by 10×.

steps.text: Off: the wide-gap oxide film is depleted; leakage is below 10⁻¹⁹ A/µm, so a pixel holds its charge for seconds.
The bottom gate draws electrons into the film next to the gate insulator (accumulation, not inversion).
Electrons move through overlapping metal s-orbitals, which stay conductive even in an amorphous film.
Low-temperature processing on large glass panels makes IGZO the switch behind OLED and high-refresh LCD pixels.

devices.where: Displays (phones, TVs, laptops); research into oxide DRAM and back-end-of-line logic.

devices.name: Floating-gate flash memory cell
devices.who: D. Kahng, S. M. Sze (Bell Labs, 1967); flash: F. Masuoka (Toshiba, 1980s)
devices.summary: A MOSFET with an extra, electrically isolated floating gate buried in its oxide. Electrons pushed onto the floating gate by tunnelling raise the threshold voltage; reading checks whether the cell turns on at a reference gate voltage.

steps.text: Erased cell, low gate: behaves like an ordinary MOSFET below threshold.
Programming: a high control-gate voltage pulls electrons through the thin tunnel oxide (Fowler–Nordheim) onto the floating gate.
The trapped electrons stay for 10+ years; their charge raises V_T by several volts.
Read: at a middle gate voltage an erased cell conducts (1) and a programmed one does not (0). Multi-level cells store 3–4 bits per cell.

devices.where: Every SSD, phone, memory card and microcontroller program memory.
